stem: A client reports recurrent, sudden, severe, electric shock-like pain on one side of the face that lasts seconds and can be triggered by chewing, talking, tooth brushing, or light touch. Which condition is most consistent with this pattern?
rationale: NCBI StatPearls describes trigeminal neuralgia as recurrent, brief, severe, electric shock-like unilateral facial pain that may be triggered by innocuous stimuli such as light touch, tooth brushing, chewing, talking, or face washing. This triggerable paroxysmal pattern is much more characteristic of trigeminal neuralgia than migraine, otitis media, or temporomandibular joint disorder. A detailed oral and neurologic evaluation is still appropriate because other causes of facial pain must be excluded.
educational_objective: Recognize brief, unilateral, electric shock-like facial pain triggered by innocuous facial or oral stimuli as the characteristic clinical pattern of trigeminal neuralgia.
source_organization: National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI Bookshelf)
source_version_date: Last update March 3, 2024; accessed and currentness-rechecked 2026-08-16
source_locator: Introduction; History and Physical — paroxysmal electric shock-like pain and trigger zones; Evaluation — ICHD-3 criteria including brief severe electric shock-like pain precipitated by innocuous stimuli
source_claim_supported: Trigeminal neuralgia presents as recurrent brief unilateral electric shock-like facial pain, often triggered by innocuous stimuli including light touch, chewing, talking, and tooth brushing.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Printed p.14, Physiological Adaptation — recognize manifestations of altered neurologic function and acute/chronic physiological conditions

source_original.stem: A client reports sudden, severe, brief episodes of stabbing facial pain triggered by activities such as chewing, talking, or light touch to the face, and initially assumes this must be a dental problem needing a dentist visit. The nurse should recognize this as potentially consistent with:

options.A: A routine dental disorder causing continuous pain unrelated to facial triggers
options.B: Trigeminal neuralgia causing brief, severe facial pain triggered by light stimuli
options.C: Migraine causing prolonged throbbing headache rather than brief facial shocks
options.D: Otitis media causing persistent ear pain rather than triggered facial shocks

source_original.rationale: Trigeminal neuralgia is characterized by sudden, severe, brief episodes of stabbing or electric shock-like facial pain along the distribution of the trigeminal nerve, often triggered by routine activities such as chewing, talking, or light touch, distinct from the more prolonged, throbbing pain typical of migraine.
source_original.source_detail: Clinical presentation: sudden brief electric-shock-like facial pain triggered by benign stimuli; 2025 review, accessed 2026-08-14.

correction_summary: Replaced the secondary AAFP source with NCBI StatPearls, removed meta-explanatory distractor wording that cued the answer, made all options diagnosis labels, retained the exact trigger pattern, and reduced difficulty from hard to easy.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Cranial nerve V pain syndrome / trigeminal neuralgia
audit_findings.currentness: NCBI chapter last updated 2024-03-03; current search found no conflicting newer authoritative diagnostic criteria.
audit_findings.claim_audit: The final stem reproduces the NCBI/ICHD-3-supported paroxysmal duration, severity, shock-like quality, unilateral distribution, and innocuous-stimulus triggers without adding unsupported precision.

distractor_audit.A: Correct and directly matches the characteristic pattern.
distractor_audit.B: Migraine is not characterized by seconds-long touch-triggered facial shocks.
distractor_audit.C: Otitis media produces otologic pain/findings rather than trigger-zone paroxysms.
distractor_audit.D: TMJ disorder can cause facial/jaw pain but not the classic brief electric shock-like innocuous-trigger pattern.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Dental pain can mimic facial pain, but the recurrent seconds-long shock-like attacks triggered by light stimuli are characteristic of trigeminal neuralgia; no competing option matches all features.
audit_findings.cueing: Final options are concise diagnosis labels of similar form; the answer must be selected from the symptom pattern rather than explanatory wording.
audit_findings.blueprint: Physiological Adaptation is appropriate for recognition of altered neurologic function.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Re-solved the item against dental, migraine, otologic, and TMJ causes; rechecked NCBI History/Physical and ICHD-3 criteria; A remained uniquely correct after cueing cleanup.
